findings.claim: There is exactly one write path per delivery attempt — no code path writes to webhook_delivery and a second system in the same operation, so reliability-resilience.d (transaction-boundary correctness across dual writes) is legitimately not-applicable here, not a gap

limitations: Cannot observe actual runtime failure behavior (e.g., whether the JAX-RS client's post() call fully returns before the transaction's commit boundary) — this is inferred from the code structure (POST call site is inside the @Transactional method, before the entity mutations), not from an observed incident.

findings.claim: DeliveryRetryJob resends the identical payload to a subscriber on every retry with no idempotency key or header, so a subscriber that already processed a request but whose acknowledgment was lost will receive and potentially reprocess a duplicate
findings.doc_source: no explicit doc claim — evaluated directly against code

findings.explanation: Any retry-on-failure design needs the retried operation to be safely repeatable by whoever's on the receiving end; here the receiving end (a third-party subscriber) has no way to recognize a retried delivery as a duplicate of one it may have already processed, because nothing distinguishing identifies the attempt from the original.
findings.recommendation: Send a stable idempotency key (e.g. the delivery row's own UUID id) as a header on every attempt, and document the expectation that subscribers dedupe on it.

findings.claim: DomainEventConsumer has no event-level dedup (no unique constraint or idempotency key derived from the source Kafka event) — a Kafka at-least-once redelivery of the same event would create a second, duplicate set of webhook_delivery rows
findings.doc_source: no explicit doc claim — evaluated directly against code

evidence.note: new WebhookDelivery(UUID.randomUUID(), ...) — a fresh random id is generated per invocation, with nothing tying it back to the source Kafka event/offset for dedup

findings.explanation: This is distinct from f36 (which is about the delivery-side retry, not ingestion): if the consumer crashes after persisting delivery rows but before its Kafka offset commits (an ordinary at-least-once redelivery scenario, not an edge case), the same domain event will be reprocessed and a second full set of delivery rows created for every subscriber, each independently delivered.
findings.recommendation: Derive a deterministic idempotency key from the source Kafka event (e.g. topic+partition+offset, or an event id if the payload carries one) and add a unique constraint so a redelivered event can't create duplicate delivery rows.
limitations: Whether Kafka redelivery actually occurs in practice depends on the consumer's commit-strategy configuration, which uses the connector's defaults here (not overridden in application.properties) — this finding is about the code's lack of a dedup mechanism, which matters regardless of how often redelivery actually happens at the configured commit strategy.

findings.claim: DeliverySender.attempt has no per-call timeout or circuit breaker, so a single hanging subscriber can stall the entire single-threaded DeliveryRetryJob run, delaying every other pending delivery in that batch

evidence.note: no timeout on the JAX-RS client
for (WebhookDelivery delivery : due) processes up to BATCH_SIZE deliveries sequentially, one deliverySender.attempt() call at a time, inside one @Scheduled run

findings.explanation: Distinct from f31 (which frames this as a cost-guardrail inconsistency): this is the availability-cascade consequence specifically — because the retry loop is sequential and single-threaded per run, one unresponsive target_url with no timeout can block the entire run indefinitely, meaning every other subscriber's pending deliveries in that batch are delayed by however long that one hang lasts, with no isolation between subscribers.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-call timeout (even a generous one, e.g. 10-30s) to DeliverySender's client so one hanging subscriber can't block delivery to every other subscriber in the same run.

findings.claim: The domain-events consumer has no dead-letter topic and no failure-strategy override, meaning an unhandled exception in onEvent() (e.g. a persistence failure) would be handled by the messaging connector's default failure strategy, which can halt the channel rather than skip the one bad message

evidence.note: @Incoming("domain-events") has no failure-strategy attribute; application.properties has no mp.messaging.incoming.domain-events.failure-strategy override either

findings.explanation: SmallRye Reactive Messaging's Kafka connector default failure strategy on an unhandled exception is to fail (stop) the channel rather than skip-and-continue, unless explicitly configured otherwise — none of the other options (ignore, dead-letter-queue) are configured here. Combined with f33/f34 (zero observability on this path), a single malformed event or transient persistence error could silently halt all future event ingestion for this service until an operator notices independently and restarts it.
findings.recommendation: Configure an explicit failure-strategy (at minimum a dead-letter-topic, so a bad message is quarantined rather than either dropped silently or killing the whole channel), and add a counter on consumer failures so this is operator-visible if it happens.
limitations: The exact default failure-strategy behavior depends on the SmallRye Reactive Messaging Kafka connector version in use, which isn't pinned to a specific version anywhere visible in this repo (build.gradle uses the Quarkus BOM without an explicit connector version) — the 'fail-the-channel' default is the well-documented SmallRye Kafka behavior as of recent Quarkus versions, but this repo doesn't let it be pinned down further.

findings.claim: The disclosed retry-ceiling gap (infinite retry, no FAILED transition, no dead-letter path) leaves this service with no actual recovery mechanism for a permanently-undeliverable event, and — because of f33/f34's observability gap — no way for an operator to notice it happening except by directly querying the database
findings.doc_location: "Known gap: retries have no ceiling", lines 23-30

evidence.note: same evidence as f18 — no cap, no FAILED transition

findings.explanation: The doc is honest that current low volume has kept this from causing an incident, which is why severity is kept at medium rather than high — but the gap is compounded by having zero visibility into it (f33/f34): even when it does start accumulating (e.g. after a subscriber decommissions an endpoint without unsubscribing), nothing in this service will surface it.
findings.recommendation: Add an attempt_count ceiling with a transition to FAILED, and — regardless of whether the ceiling fix ships immediately — add a gauge/alert on count of rows with attempt_count above some threshold, so the gap is operator-visible even before it's closed.

findings.claim: DomainEvent's deserialization has no explicit lenient/unknown-field configuration, so a producer adding a new field to the event payload could break consumer deserialization depending on the runtime Jackson configuration's default strictness
findings.doc_source: no explicit doc claim — evaluated directly against code

evidence.note: public record DomainEvent(String type, String payload) {} — no @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) or equivalent lenient-deserialization annotation

findings.explanation: Whether this actually breaks on a new field depends on the Jackson/Quarkus runtime configuration's default strictness, which isn't visible or overridden anywhere in this repo — this finding is about the absence of an explicit forward-compatibility guarantee at the code level, not a confirmed runtime failure.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit unknown-field tolerance (or confirm and document the runtime default) so producers can safely add fields to the event payload without a coordinated consumer deploy.
limitations: Actual deserialization strictness depends on Quarkus/Jackson runtime configuration not visible in this repo (no explicit ObjectMapper customization found) — this is a contract-shape observation, not an observed runtime failure.

findings.claim: (Architectural evaluation) The single externally-reachable HTTP entry point in this service is protected by one global, no-opt-out authentication filter, giving it consistent auth coverage by construction rather than by convention

evidence.note: @Provider @Priority(Priorities.AUTHENTICATION) — a global JAX-RS filter with no per-resource opt-in mechanism visible anywhere

findings.explanation: Because the filter is registered globally rather than annotated per-resource, there's no way for a future new endpoint to accidentally launch unprotected — the inconsistency this check usually looks for (some endpoints protected, siblings not) is structurally prevented here rather than just currently true by coincidence.

findings.claim: DeliverySender posts to target_url exactly as resolved from SubscriptionRegistryClient with no validation of scheme or host, so a compromised or misconfigured subscription-registry entry could direct this service to make requests to internal infrastructure

evidence.note: client.target(targetUrl) — targetUrl is used directly with no scheme allow-list, no private/internal-IP blocklist, no host validation of any kind

findings.explanation: target_url crosses a real trust boundary: it originates from a separate service (subscription-registry) and is trusted implicitly by DeliverySender, which will POST the domain event's payload to whatever URL that service returns. If subscription-registry is ever compromised, misconfigured, or has a validation gap of its own that lets a subscriber register an internal-network URL, this service becomes a vector for making authenticated-looking outbound requests to internal infrastructure (an SSRF-shaped risk) — and per f34, such a request would produce no operator-visible signal either way.
findings.recommendation: Validate target_url before use (https-only, reject private/loopback/link-local IP ranges and cloud metadata addresses) either in this service or, more centrally, at write-time in subscription-registry, and treat this as a cross-service trust-boundary decision that needs to be made explicitly rather than left implicit.
limitations: Whether subscription-registry itself validates target_url on write is out of scope for this repo — this finding is about the absence of any validation on the receiving/using side, which is a defense-in-depth gap regardless of what the other service does.
